basis: Ten development conversations (43 raw Apertus replies), 43 prefix-local turn evaluations, 10 conversation reviews, 7 selected D1 prefixes with 56 branch candidates judged in blinded fours. Ten conversations cannot establish rates; these are case readings.

directions.direction: 1. Adaptive simulated user (react to the actual reply, change strategy, help, accept, abandon)
directions.evidence: All twelve moves occurred across 28 user turns (point_to_defect 8, give_example 3, simplify 5, clarify 4, add_context 1, decompose 1, express_frustration 3, restate 1, continue 3, accept_partial 1, finish 3, abandon 6); no policy deviation and no repair call was needed; the reviewer found no oracle leak in any of the ten conversations and confirmed that user turns reacted to visible defects. The ME021 pattern did not repeat: only one restatement occurred in the whole run, and after failures the users pointed to the precise defect, gave two-line examples, narrowed the request or left. Change required: finish and abandon produce no public message, so the conversation's end exists only in private metadata; the reviewer raised this in five conversations. Production should emit a short closing utterance for terminal moves. Second, smaller change: assistance_level was under-reported on six turns (the reviewer corrected none→pointed_defect or partial_scaffold); derive it from the review or constrain it in the schema.

directions.direction: 2. Selection of preference points on saved trajectories (prevention, supported recovery, healthy continuation)
directions.evidence: Points were found where they existed and nowhere else: 21 possible points over ten conversations, no forced cells; DVI004 produced a prevention point but no supported recovery because the user only restated (correctly recorded rather than invented); RGD003 produced only a healthy continuation because no serious error occurred; RGD005's two points are held for the specialist maths judge. Mechanically the protocol held: byte-identical prefixes and matching hashes at sampling and judging, blinded fours, no pair mixing replies from before and after a hint, no suffix splicing. Yield is the caveat: 1 accepted pair from 7 points at 8 candidates, and the verification step rejected one judge-selected chosen reply that broke a checkable constraint (DVI001 prevention). Report this as 'no verified acceptable reply within 8', not as incapacity: the pilot needed 12–16 samples for 6 of 14 prefixes. Production should sample 16 up front on these hard cells, as the pilot recommended.

directions.direction: 3. Reference-guided categories (writing, troubleshooting, learning) as a separate demo
directions.call: retain writing and troubleshooting; change learning
directions.evidence: Access separation held everywhere: no hidden diagnosis, gold transfer answer or reference draft reached the user simulator or Apertus in any of the 43 replies (leak check on every request, plus the reviewer's own reading). The troubleshooting worlds stayed consistent, including when the assistant went off-script: RGD003 reached the fixed resolution and RGD004 was resolved at turn 4 after three wrong replies, with every observation coming from the fixed table. Writing produced the intended behaviour (undisclosed preferences never counted against earlier replies; revealed later as new preferences). Learning needs two changes: RGD005's mathematics must go to the specialist maths judge (all six replies carry maths content and are held here, and the transfer check never fired because the learner was never taught correctly), and RGD002-style illustrative drafts must be written strictly within the evaluator's own no-invented-extras rule, which the reviewer found my draft breached in small ways.

answers.question: Did helpful guidance arise plausibly rather than through hidden oracle knowledge?
answers.answer: Yes in all ten conversations. The reviewer found no oracle leak; troubleshooting users reported only observations produced by the fixed world for the steps they took, and the writing users' examples were their own short phrases, never the illustrative draft.

answers.question: Did the user react to a real defect instead of a scripted complaint?
answers.answer: Yes, with one exception: in DVI001 the user repeatedly claimed the draft was under 220 words when it was about 235 (a simulator error, recorded). Every other complaint matched a defect the turn evaluation also found.

answers.question: Did some conversations progress without failure?
answers.answer: Partly. RGD003 completed with no serious error (two turns, natural completion). DVI004, RGD001, RGD002, RGD004 and RGD006 had at least one good or minor turn before a failure. RGD005 failed at every turn.

answers.question: Did the assistant use guidance, retain earlier constraints and finish the task?
answers.answer: Rarely. 28 of 43 replies were serious, 11 minor, 4 good. The dominant failure is repeating a rejected reply verbatim under precise correction (DVI001, DVI002, DVI003, RGD001), and inventing facts (RGD002 refreshments, RGD004 an invented VS Code 'Isolated Mode', DVI004 a wrong entrance). Four conversations reached the user's goal (DVI004, RGD003, RGD004, and partially RGD001).

answers.question: Did the simulator remain consistent, including when the assistant went off-script?
answers.answer: Yes for the worlds and learner states; the reviewer's residual findings are labelling (assistance level, one move label) and the invisible terminal turn, plus the DVI001 word-count slip.

answers.question: For learning, did the learner attempt demonstrate progress on an unsupplied example?
answers.answer: No. RGD005 never received a sound explanation, so no transfer attempt was made and the misconception stayed; RGD006 showed limited, teaching-supported progress (selection and merging) but the learner never produced an independent summary. The design produced the evidence needed to say this; the model did not teach.

answers.question: Did a 'positive' answer still contain incorrect factual or mathematical claims?
answers.answer: Yes in seven conversations, listed per case in the review page: RGD005 turn 3 reaches the correct value 4 through false equalities, DVI003 turn 5 invents execution dates, RGD002 turn 1 promises refreshments, RGD004 turn 4 adds an invalid Windows command. This is why verification sits after the ranking judge: it rejected the chosen reply at DVI001's prevention point.

failures: Simulator: terminal moves (finish/abandon) leave no public message, so an ending is only in metadata (five conversations flagged).
Simulator: assistance_level under-reported on six user turns; one move label (RGD003 turn 1 clarify vs continue, RGD006 turn 4 accept_partial vs abandon) corrected by the reviewer.
Simulator: DVI001's user asserted a word count that was wrong (about 235 words called 'under 220').
Seed authoring: DVI003's user turn 4 asked to leave three bullets unchanged while also moving content out of one of them; RGD002's illustrative draft contains small extras beyond the supplied facts.
Maths: RGD005's six turns carry maths content and are held for the specialist maths judge; nothing here decides their eligibility.
Yield: 6 of 7 selected prefixes produced no verified acceptable reply within 8 candidates. This is a bound on this run, not a measure of the model's capability.

Scope: ten conversations, one checkpoint, one judge (Sol with rubric v2.4 plus a verification pass); no trained-model comparison; no DPO trainer exists, so completion-only masking is declared, not verified.
Two conversations ended at the turn cap (RGD002, RGD005) and none hit the context limit at the 1,024-token reply cap; DVI002 ended after three turns because the user's patience is low by design.
